The ranat thum lek (Thai: ระนาดทุ้มเหล็ก, pronounced [ranâːt tʰúm lèk]) is a metallophone used in Thai classical music. It is the larger of Thailand's two metallophones; the smaller is called the ranat ek. The ranat thum lek consists of flat metal bars laid on a rectangular wooden resonator. It is played with two bamboo sticks with padded tips. The origin of this instrument is credited to a brother of King Rama IV (1854–1868), at the same time as the treble metallophone was created. The ranat thum lek is very similar to the bronze roneat of Cambodia.

The low metallophone was then widely used in Thai classical court music and became indispensable. Its influence spread to neighbouring regions, forming an instrument system similar to Cambodia's bronze roneat, which shows the exchange and blending of Southeast Asian musical cultures.
